segments.text: Before the new one: say "sorrow, distress" (bādha), "comfort, ease" (sukhaṁ) and "a story" (katha). Then "my bag is lost". (nā sañci pōyindi.)
దుఃఖం — duḥkhaṁ — "grief".
ఆ కథ చదివి నాకు దుఃఖం వచ్చింది. ā katha cadivi nāku duḥkhaṁ vaccindi. — "Reading that story, I was moved to grief."
బాధ is the everyday hurt and sadness of a bad day. దుఃఖం (duḥkhaṁ) is heavier: grief, the sorrow that brings tears. Like a fever, it "comes" to you: నాకు దుఃఖం (duḥkhaṁ) వచ్చింది.
The mark after దు is a breath, ḥ. Many speakers let it run into the next sound, close to dukkhaṁ. The next lesson puts the mark in your hand.

దుఃఖం (duḥkhaṁ) is borrowed from Sanskrit duḥkha, "difficulty, pain" (CDIAL 6375), with Telugu's noun ending -ం. CDIAL notes it was formed after sukha, the word you know as సుఖం: the two are a pair, ease and its opposite.

lessons.title: ః (ḥ) — the visarga inside దుఃఖం (duḥkhaṁ)
lessons.gloss: the visarga ః — the two dots inside దుఃఖం

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
your eyes or your hands for the steps that ask you to read, point, write or gesture
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on, your eyes, for letter shapes on the page and your eyes or your hands for the steps that ask you to read, point, write or gesture. You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach them, but leave these sections until you have stopped: Warm-up, Script you'll notice: ః and Guided Practice.

segments.text: Before the new one: write ం and ఖ once each, and name them. (The sunna, ṁ, and kha.)
Now say దుఃఖం (duḥkhaṁ), "grief". Both of those are in it. This lesson takes out the one mark you have not written and puts it in your hand.
ః — the visarga, ḥ: a short breath after a vowel. It is two small rings, one above the other, written after its syllable: దు + ః becomes దుః, duḥ.
Do not confuse it with ం, one ring, which is ṁ. The visarga lives in words taken from Sanskrit, and most of them are learned words; దుఃఖం (duḥkhaṁ) is the one you will meet most.
Write ః (ḥ) yourself, slowly, and larger than it is printed: two small rings the same size, one above the other, both on the right of the syllable they follow.

This book does not yet say where the pen starts on this shape, or which way it travels. That is taught with real variation from school to school, and it waits here until it can be written down from a source. Copying the printed shape needs no such source, and it puts the shape in your hand in the meantime.

lessons.title: నాకు భయంగా ఉంది (nāku bhayaṅgā undi) — how I feel
lessons.gloss: I feel afraid — feelings with the dative and -గా ఉంది

segments.text: Say "fear" (bhayaṁ), "anger" (kōpaṁ) and "happily" (santōṣaṅgā). Then say "grief". (duḥkhaṁ.)

segments.instruction: ః (ḥ), once

blocks.title: You'll want to know: నాకు … -గా ఉంది

segments.text: నాకు చాలా సంతోషంగా ఉంది. nāku cālā santōṣaṅgā undi. — "I am very happy."
నాకు భయంగా ఉంది. nāku bhayaṅgā undi. — "I am afraid."

The one who feels is in the dative, నాకు, as in నాకు తెలుగు వచ్చు. The feeling takes -గా, and ఉంది, "it is", closes the sentence: "to me, fearfully, it is". So too నాకు బాధగా ఉంది, "I feel sad"; నాకు చలిగా ఉంది, "I feel cold"; నాకు ఆకలిగా ఉంది, "I am hungry".
Some feelings "come" instead, like the grief of the last lesson: > నాకు కోపం వచ్చింది.
nāku kōpaṁ vaccindi. — "I got angry."

blocks.title: You'll want to know: … అనిపించింది, I felt

segments.text: రాత్రి ఒంటరిగా నడుస్తున్నప్పుడు నాకు భయంగా అనిపించింది. rātri oṇṭarigā naḍustunnappuḍu nāku bhayaṅgā anipiñcindi. — "Walking alone at night, I felt afraid."

For how a moment felt, put the -గా feeling before అనిపించింది, "it seemed": "to me, fearfully, it seemed". ఒంటరిగా (oṇṭarigā, "alone"). The scene is the -తున్నప్పుడు of a story; the feeling is the event in it.

lessons.title: వెళ్ళాలని ఉంది (veḷḷālani undi) — what I would like
lessons.gloss: I would like to go — wishes, hopes and dreams with -ఆలని

segments.text: Say "I must go" (nēnu veḷḷāli) and "I am happy" (nāku santōṣaṅgā undi). Then "a dream", "hope" and "a wish". (kala, āśa, kōrika.)

blocks.title: You'll want to know: నాకు … -ఆలని ఉంది

segments.text: నాకు తెలుగు బాగా నేర్చుకోవాలని ఉంది. nāku telugu bāgā nērcukōvālani undi. — "I would like to learn Telugu well."
నాకు మా ఊరికి వెళ్ళాలని ఉంది. nāku mā ūriki veḷḷālani undi. — "I would like to go to my home town."
Take the -ఆలి of "must", add అని, "saying": వెళ్ళాలి + అని becomes వెళ్ళాలని. Then నాకు … ఉంది: "to me there is (the thought) that I must go". The wish sits in the dative, like a feeling.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: my wish, my dream, my hope

segments.text: తెలుగులో ఒక పుస్తకం రాయాలని నా కోరిక. telugulō oka pustakaṁ rāyālani nā kōrika. — "My wish is to write a book in Telugu."
వైద్యుడు కావాలని నా కల. vaidyuḍu kāvālani nā kala. — "My dream is to become a doctor."
ఆ ఉద్యోగం వస్తుందని నా ఆశ. ā udyōgaṁ vastundani nā āśa. — "My hope is that I will get that job."
The wish comes first, closed by -ఆలని or -అని; నా కోరిక, నా కల or నా ఆశ comes last. In కావాలని, కా- has its plain sense, "to become". A job "comes" to you: ఉద్యోగం వస్తుంది.
